slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body: Cache Memory
slides.notes: First of all we'll be learning about the Cache Memory.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
The Problem We're Solving
Every trip there wastes precious cooking time
slides.notes: Now, before understanding cache memory, let's first look at the problem. The processor often needs to access data from the main memory, and every such trip takes time. Just like repeatedly going to the pantry while cooking slows the process, frequent memory access also results in wasted processing time.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
The Problem We're Solving
That "counter" is what we call cache memory 
What if the chef kept the ingredients they use most often on the counter, right next to them?
slides.notes: Next, instead of walking to the pantry every time, imagine the chef keeps the most frequently used ingredients right on the kitchen counter. This makes them instantly available whenever needed. Similarly, cache memory acts like that counter by keeping frequently accessed information close to the CPU for quicker access.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Introduction
Cache is very fast memory located close to the CPU
Stores frequently used data and instructions
Reduces the time CPU waits for RAM and helps the CPU run faster and smoother
Cache
Frequently used data 
Instructions
slides.notes: Now, cache memory is a small but extremely fast memory placed close to the CPU. It keeps the data and instructions that the processor accesses repeatedly, so they are readily available whenever needed. This minimizes the CPU's wait for data from RAM, resulting in faster and smoother execution.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Why Is It Needed?
A modern CPU executes an instruction in ~0.3 ns (≈3 GHz clock)
A single RAM access takes ~50–100 ns
That means the CPU could run ~150–300 instructions in the time it waits for one memory access
If the CPU waited for RAM every time → performance collapses
Cache sits in between and absorbs most of these waits
CPU is much faster than RAM — this isn't a small gap, it's orders of magnitude
slides.notes: Moving on, the need for cache memory comes from the huge speed difference between the CPU and RAM. While the CPU can execute instructions in a fraction of a nanosecond, accessing data from RAM takes much longer. During this time, the CPU has to wait instead of processing instructions. Cache helps bridge this speed gap by reducing these waiting periods, improving overall performance.

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body: Locality of Reference
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Locality of Reference.

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body:
What Does It Actually Mean?
Locality of reference is the tendency of a running program to access the same small set of memory locations — or locations near each other — repeatedly, over a short window of time
slides.notes: Now, before understanding how cache works, let's look at the idea behind it. Most programs don't access random memory locations all the time. Instead, they tend to reuse the same memory locations or nearby ones repeatedly within a short period.This behavior is known as locality of reference, and it is the reason cache memory is so effective.

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body:
What Does It Actually Mean?
Programs don't access memory randomly; they access it in patterns
This is the entire reason caching works at all 
If every memory access were random, keeping a small fast cache would give almost no benefit
slides.notes: Now, the key idea here is that programs usually follow a predictable memory access pattern. Since the required data is often related or repeatedly used, the cache can keep it ready for quick access. If memory requests were completely unpredictable, the cache would rarely be useful.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Locality of Reference
Spatial Locality
Cache
Temporal Locality
(same location again)
(nearby locations next)
slides.notes: Moving on, locality of reference is broadly classified into two types.Temporal locality focuses on reusing the same memory location within a short time, while spatial locality refers to accessing memory locations that are close to one another. We'll understand each of these in detail now.

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body:
1. Temporal Locality
If a memory location was accessed recently, it's likely to be accessed again soon
All get touched over and over in a short span
slides.notes: Next, temporal locality is based on the idea that recently accessed data is likely to be needed again very soon. This is common with loop counters, frequently used variables, and functions that are called repeatedly. Since these memory locations are reused often, keeping them in the cache speeds up execution.

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body:
In a for loop that runs 1,000 times, the loop counter variable i is accessed on every single iteration
Cache exploits this by keeping recently-used data close by, so the next request for it is fast
1. Temporal Locality

slides.notes: Now, let's understand temporal locality with an example. In a loop, the loop counter is accessed repeatedly during every iteration. Instead of fetching it from the main memory each time, the cache keeps it readily available, allowing the processor to access it much faster.

slides.notes: Now, let's understand Temporal Locality. In the first access, the CPU retrieves X from main memory, which is comparatively slower, and a copy of it is placed in cache memory. If the CPU needs X again shortly after, it can access it directly from the cache, resulting in much faster execution. This repeated access to recently used data is known as Temporal Locality.

slides.body: Analogy

Using the same spoon repeatedly while eating a meal — you don't grab a new spoon after every bite; you reach for the one you just used because you know you'll need it again in seconds.
SO similarly we use the same memory locations in case of the Temporal Locality

slides.title: Locality of Reference
slides.body:
2. Spatial Locality
If a memory location was accessed, nearby locations are likely to be accessed soon after
Stored in adjacent memory, accessing one element usually means the next one is coming
Sequential instruction execution
Structured data
slides.notes: Moving on, spatial locality means a program is likely to access nearby memory locations one after another. This is commonly seen while traversing arrays, where elements are stored next to each other. The same behavior is observed during sequential instruction execution and when working with structured data, allowing the cache to fetch nearby information efficiently.

As a result, if these neighboring locations are needed next, the CPU can retrieve them directly from the cache, making memory access much faster.

Types of Cache
Caching isn't unique to the CPU — it's a general idea used in several places in a computer system:
slides.notes: Now, the idea of caching is not limited to the CPU alone. It's a general technique used throughout a computer system wherever faster access to frequently used data is needed. Now, we'll explore the different types of cache and where each one is used.

slides.notes: This diagram shows how cache memory is organized inside a modern CPU. Each CPU core has its own dedicated L1 and L2 cache, allowing it to access frequently used data quickly. Below them is the L3 cache, which is shared by all the CPU cores. If the required data is not available in any cache level, the CPU finally accesses the main memory, which takes comparatively more time.This layered organization helps reduce memory access time and improves the overall system performance.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body: Disk Cache
slides.notes: Now, let's understand Disk Cache. Unlike CPU Cache, which stores frequently used CPU data, Disk Cache stores frequently accessed disk blocks to reduce the number of slow disk accesses. The operating system maintains a page cache in main memory, while the Hard Disk or SSD also contains a small onboard buffer for temporarily holding data. When the CPU requests data, it is first checked in these caches before accessing the actual storage. This helps improve disk read and write performance by reducing access time.

Otherwise, the request is forwarded to the web server. This reduces network traffic and provides faster access to frequently visited websites

If the same website is requested again before the cache expires, the resolver returns the IP address directly, making website access much faster.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body:
Inside CPU Cache
By Level
How far it sits from the CPU core (L1, L2, L3)
CPU Cache itself isn't one single block — it's organized in two independent ways
By Type
What it actually stores (Instruction, Data, Unified)
CPU Cache
slides.notes:
Moving on, the CPU cache has its own internal organization and isn't treated as a single memory block.
 It can be understood from two perspectives: by type, which tells us what kind of information the cache stores,
 and by level, which indicates how close the cache is to the CPU core. We'll look at both of these one by one.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body:
Why Multiple Levels?
A cache can't be both very fast and very large 
Speed and size trade off, and cost per byte rises sharply as memory gets faster
slides.notes: Moving on, designing a cache always involves a trade-off. If we try to make it very large, accessing data takes longer. On the other hand, making it very fast significantly increases the cost per byte. Since a single cache cannot optimize speed, size, and cost at the same time, processors organize the cache into multiple levels to achieve a practical balance.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body:
Why Multiple Levels?
So CPUs use a hierarchy — several caches stacked by distance from the core
Each level trades a bit of speed for a lot more capacity as you move outward
slides.notes: Next, instead of relying on a single cache, processors organize cache into a hierarchy of multiple levels. As we move farther away from the CPU core, each cache level offers more capacity, but at the cost of a little speed.This layered approach helps the processor balance fast access with enough storage for frequently used data.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body: Levels of Cache
tables: Fastest, smallest, private to the core; usually split into L1-instruction and L1-data
Per-core or shared by a couple of cores
Larger, a bit slower than L1
Largest, slowest cache — but still far faster than RAM (~200+ cycles)

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Trade-off rule
 The closer to the CPU, the faster but smaller and costlier per byte
The Compromise between speed and size, rather than one cache trying (and failing) to be both
More levels = a balanced compromise
slides.notes: Now, if we tried to build a single cache that was extremely fast while also storing a huge amount of data, it simply wouldn't be practical. Hardware designers therefore split the responsibility across different cache levels. The smaller caches handle requests that need the quickest response, while the larger ones keep more data available whenever the upper levels don't have it. This approach gives the processor good overall performance without relying on one perfect cache.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Types of CPU Cache
Splitting instruction/data caches lets the CPU fetch an instruction and access data at the same time — needed for pipelining
A single unified cache would force both to queue behind each other
slides.notes: Moving on, the processor performs two activities continuously—it fetches the next instruction while also reading or writing the data required to execute it. If both operations depended on the same cache, one would have to wait for the other, creating unnecessary delays. To avoid this, processors typically maintain separate Instruction and Data Caches, allowing both operations to happen simultaneously and supporting efficient pipelining. In some designs, a Unified Cache is also used, where instructions and data share the same cache space.

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Imagine a library with two separate sections—one for reading books and another for borrowing reference materials. People reading books don't have to wait behind those borrowing materials. Similarly, the CPU uses separate paths for instructions and data, so fetching one doesn't delay the other.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body:
How Levels and Types Combine
Instruction Cache 
L1
Data Cache 
L1, almost always split into Instruction + Data
L2 and L3, almost always unified
slides.notes: This diagram shows how different cache levels are organized. L1 Cache is typically divided into an Instruction Cache and a Data Cache, allowing the CPU to fetch instructions and access data simultaneously. However, L2 and L3 are usually unified caches, meaning they store both instructions and data in the same cache. This organization provides a good balance between high-speed access at L1 and efficient cache utilization at the lower levels.

slides.title: Cache Organization
slides.body:
How Levels and Types Combine
Splitting only pays off closest to the core, where speed matters most; unified is simpler and used further out, where capacity matters more than parallel access
slides.notes: Now, processors don't organize every cache level in the same way because each level has a different purpose. The first level is optimized to respond as quickly as possible, so separating instructions and data helps avoid unnecessary waiting. Once we move to the lower levels, the emphasis shifts toward keeping more information available, making a single shared cache a more practical and efficient design.

slides.title: Cache Performance
slides.body: Cache Performance
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Cache Performance

slides.title: Cache Memory
slides.body:
Cache Hit & Cache Miss
Cache Hit 
Data found in cache
Fast access
Cache Miss
Data not in cache
Must fetch from RAM
Hit Ratio: (Number of Hits) / (Total Accesses)
Cache Line/Block: Unit of data transfer between cache and memory
Miss Ratio: 1 - Hit Ratio
slides.notes: Moving on, every memory request is checked against the cache first. If the required information is already available, it's a cache hit, allowing the processor to continue without delay. Otherwise, it's a cache miss, and the data must be fetched from the main memory before execution can proceed. The overall effectiveness of the cache is measured using the Hit Ratio, while the remaining accesses are represented by the Miss Ratio. Also, data is transferred between the cache and main memory in fixed-size units called cache lines or cache blocks, rather than one byte at a time.

slides.title: Cache Hit & Cache Miss
slides.body:
Analogy
 You find pen on your desk = Hit
 You search whole house = Miss
Higher hit rate = Better performance
slides.notes: Imagine you're looking for a pen. If you find it immediately on your desk, you get it quickly with very little effort. This is similar to a Cache Hit, where the required data is found in the cache. However, if the pen isn't on the desk and you have to search the entire house, it takes much longer. This is similar to a Cache Miss, where the CPU has to retrieve the data from the slower main memory. Therefore, a higher cache hit rate results in better overall system performance.

slides.title: Cache Line/Block
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Imagine you need a pen from a storage room. Instead of bringing back just one pen every time, you bring the entire box of pens to your desk. If you need another pen later, it's already within reach, so you don't have to return to the storage room. Similarly, when the CPU requests a memory location, the cache loads the entire cache block, not just the requested data. This reduces repeated accesses to main memory and improves overall performance.

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body: Cache Mapping
slides.notes: Next we will see Cache Mapping

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Introduction
Helps the CPU quickly find the data when needed
Mapping is important because cache is smaller than RAM → not everything can fit
Cache mapping is the method used to decide where data from RAM is stored in the cache
slides.notes: Now, since the cache is much smaller than the main memory, it isn't possible to keep a copy of every piece of data. So whenever data is brought from RAM, the processor needs a rule to decide exactly where it should be placed in the cache. This process is known as cache mapping, and it also makes it easier for the CPU to locate the required data quickly during future memory accesses.

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Types of Cache Mapping
How cache decides where to store data?
Direct Mapping
Fully Associative Mapping
Set-Associative Mapping
slides.notes: Moving on, there isn't just one way to place data into the cache. Different systems use different cache mapping techniques depending on how they balance speed, hardware complexity, and cache utilization. The three most commonly used approaches are Direct Mapping, Fully Associative Mapping, and Set-Associative Mapping. We'll now understand how each of these methods decides where data is stored and the advantages they offer.

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Direct Mapping
Each block in RAM → fixed place in cache
Simple and fast
But conflicts occur if multiple blocks want the same place
Direct Mapping
Each block in RAM → fixed place in cache
Simple and fast
But conflicts occur if multiple blocks want the same place
slides.notes: Next, let's begin with Direct Mapping, the simplest cache mapping technique. In this approach, every block in the main memory has only one predetermined location in the cache where it can be stored. Because the processor always knows exactly where to look, this method is very fast and requires simple hardware. However, if multiple memory blocks are assigned to the same cache location, they keep replacing one another, leading to conflict misses and reducing the cache's overall efficiency.

slides.title: Direct Mapping
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Each student has a fixed seat, If already taken, conflict!Let's understand Direct Mapping with a simple analogy. Imagine every student in a classroom has a fixed assigned seat. Whenever a student enters the classroom, they must sit only in their designated seat and cannot choose any other. If someone is already occupying that seat, they must leave before the new student can sit there. Similarly, in Direct Mapping, each memory block can be placed in only one specific cache line. This makes cache access simple and fast, but it can also lead to frequent replacements when multiple memory blocks map to the same cache line.

slides.body:

Offset → Exact byte inside that block

slides.notes: Now, let's see how Direct Mapping actually determines the cache location for a memory block. Every memory address is divided into three parts: the Tag, the Line Number, and the Offset. The Line Number is used to identify the exact cache line where the block can be placed, the Tag verifies whether the required memory block is currently stored in that line, and the Offset selects the specific byte within the block. In Direct Mapping, the cache line is calculated using the rule Block Number modulo Number of Cache Lines, so each memory block always maps to one fixed cache line, making lookups simple and fast.

slides.notes: The main memory address is made up of s + n bits, where n bits represent the Block Offset, used to identify the exact byte or word within a block. The remaining s bits identify the memory block. When this address is interpreted by the cache, these s bits are further divided into two parts: r bits form the Index, which selects the cache line, and the remaining s − r bits form the Tag, which is used to verify whether the required memory block is present in that cache line.

slides.notes: Moving on, unlike Direct Mapping, Fully Associative Mapping allows a memory block to be placed in any cache line. This flexibility helps avoid conflict misses and makes better use of the cache. However, since the processor has to search multiple cache lines to find the required block, the lookup process is more complex and takes longer.

slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Let's understand Fully Associative Mapping with this analogy. Imagine a classroom where students are free to sit at any available seat instead of having an assigned one. This provides maximum flexibility, but the student has to search for an empty seat before sitting down. Similarly, in Fully Associative Mapping, a memory block can be placed in any cache line. This improves cache utilization but takes more time to search for the required block.

Instead, it compares the Tag with the tags stored in all cache lines to find the required block. Once a matching tag is found, the Byte Offset identifies the exact data within that block. This approach provides maximum flexibility but requires searching all cache lines, making it slower than Direct Mapping.

Any memory block can be placed in any available cache line. Each cache line stores a Tag, which identifies the memory block currently stored in that line. slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Set-Associative Mapping
Set-Associative Mapping
Cache divided into small groups (sets)
Block can go anywhere inside its assigned set
Balance of speed and flexibility
Used in most modern CPUs
slides.notes: Moving on, Set-Associative Mapping combines the advantages of both Direct Mapping and Fully Associative Mapping. Instead of allowing a block to go anywhere in the cache or restricting it to a single location, the cache is divided into sets. Each memory block is assigned to one particular set, but within that set it can occupy any available cache line. This approach reduces conflict misses while keeping the search process efficient, which is why it is widely used in modern processors.

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Set-Associative Mapping
The cache is organized into multiple sets, and each set contains multiple lines (e.g., 2-way or 4-way)
slides.notes: Set-Associative Mapping combines the advantages of Direct Mapping and Fully Associative Mapping. Instead of treating the cache as a single collection of lines, it is divided into multiple sets, with each set containing multiple cache lines, such as 2-way or 4-way. A memory block is first mapped to a specific set, but within that set, it can be placed in any available cache line. This provides greater flexibility than Direct Mapping while requiring less searching than Fully Associative Mapping.

slides.title: Cache Mapping
slides.body:
Set-Associative Mapping
A memory block is assigned to one specific set, but it can be stored in any line within that set
slides.notes: Now, the key idea in Set-Associative Mapping is that the memory block is first assigned to a particular set. Once the correct set is identified, the block can be placed in any available line within that set. During a lookup, the processor searches only the lines of that assigned set instead of the entire cache, making the search faster while still providing flexibility in data placement.

slides.title: Set-Associative Mapping
slides.body:
Cache Address Breakdown
Tag → Identifies the memory block
Set Number → Selects the cache set
Offset → Exact byte inside the block
Main Memory Block X maps to any available line within a specific set
slides.notes:
Moving on, in Set-Associative Mapping, the memory address is divided into three parts: the Tag, Set Number, and Offset.  the Tag is used to determine whether the required memory block is present in one of the lines of that set, The Set Number identifies which cache set should be searched,
and the Offset selects the exact byte within the block. This organization limits the search to a single set, making lookups much more efficient than searching the entire cache while still allowing flexible data placement within the set.

slides.notes: This diagram illustrates a Two-Way Set-Associative Cache. Here, each set contains two cache lines, also called two ways. When a memory block is mapped, it first selects the appropriate set, but within that set, it can be placed in either Way 0 or Way 1. Each cache line stores a Tag to identify the memory block it contains. This organization reduces conflicts compared to Direct Mapping while requiring less searching than Fully Associative Mapping.

slides.title: Set-Associative Mapping
slides.body:
Worked Example With 3 quick steps
Given (simple numbers): Assume 16-bit physical addresses, 
Cache = 4 KB, Block = 16 bytes, 4-way set-associative
Offset bits — how many bytes in one block? 
16 bytes → need 4 bits to point to any byte inside it
Set bits — How many sets exist? 
4 KB ÷ (16 bytes × 4 ways) = 64 sets → need 6 bits to pick one
Tag bits — whatever's left over identifies which block it is → 6 bits
slides.notes: Let's calculate the address fields step by step. First, the Offset bits are calculated using log₂(Block Size). Since the block size is 16 bytes, the offset is 4 bits. Next, the number of sets is calculated using Cache Size ÷ (Block Size × Number of Ways), giving 64 sets. Therefore, Set bits = log₂(64) = 6 bits. Finally, the Tag bits are obtained using Address bits − Set bits − Offset bits, which gives 16 − 6 − 4 = 6 bits.

slides.title: Set-Associative Mapping
slides.body:
Worked Example
So an address breaks into: 6 (Tag) + 6 (Set) + 4 (Offset)
Applied to one address: 0010101001111011
slides.notes: Now, let's apply our calculations to this address: 0010101001111011. we divide it into 6 Tag bits, 6 Set bits, and 4 Offset bits. The first 6 bits, 001010, form the Tag, identifying Block ID 10. The next 6 bits, 100111, form the Set, indicating that the block maps to Set 39. Finally, the last 4 bits, 1011, form the Offset, identifying byte 11 within that memory block.

slides.title: Set-Associative Mapping
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Students are assigned to a specific row (the set) but can sit in any seat within that row (any line in the set). It's a middle ground — some structure like Direct Mapping (you know which row to go to), but some freedom like Fully Associative Mapping (any seat in that row works).
